issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction under the special remedy for a returning non-resident owner satisfies the required ownership period, as against a tenant who admits having been inducted by that landlord and remains in possession, without separately proving title against that tenant through documents linking the property to the leased premises.
material_facts: The landlord was a returning non-resident who sought the shop for his own use, and the court accepted his non-resident status and need for it.

The tenant admitted that he occupied the shop as a tenant under the landlord, though he disputed the year in which the tenancy began; even on the tenant’s account, the tenancy began more than five years before the eviction petition.
The tenant continued to occupy the shop and did not claim that a paramount title holder had become entitled to it or that the landlord’s title had ended after the tenancy began.
The landlord’s sale deeds had been proved, but the lower courts considered him not to have sufficiently linked them to the land beneath the shop.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from denying the landlord’s title while the tenancy continued and possession had not been surrendered. The landlord’s ownership period was therefore established as against the tenant, the lower courts’ decisions were set aside, and eviction was ordered.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Land Restriction Act, 1949 permits a returning non-resident Indian owner to seek possession of a let residential or non-residential building required for the owner’s or a dependent’s use, subject to the five-year ownership threshold and the statutory limits on exercising the right. Under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, a tenant cannot, during the tenancy, deny that the landlord had title when the tenancy began. Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, (1976) 4 SCC 184, reiterates this rule and explains that the landlord’s title is ordinarily irrelevant in an eviction suit. The stated exceptions include valid attornment to a paramount title holder and the landlord’s subsequent loss of title. These general rules of evidence and estoppel apply to tenants of non-resident Indian owners as well.

rule.if: returned_nonresident_owner_seeks_personal_use_eviction and tenant_admitted_induction_by_landlord and tenancy_continues and tenant_has_not_surrendered_possession and not tenant_shows_paramount_title_attornment and not tenant_shows_subsequent_loss_of_landlord_title

predicates.returned_nonresident_owner_seeks_persona: A returning non-resident owner seeks eviction of a tenant because the owner requires the let premises for personal use or for the use of a dependent.
predicates.tenant_admitted_induction_by_landlord: The tenant admitted that the landlord inducted the tenant into possession as a tenant, even if the tenant disputed when the tenancy began.
predicates.tenancy_continues: The landlord-tenant relationship remained in force when the title dispute was raised.
predicates.tenant_has_not_surrendered_possession: The tenant had not returned possession of the premises to the landlord.
predicates.tenant_shows_paramount_title_attornment: The tenant showed that the tenancy had been validly attorned to a person holding paramount title.
predicates.tenant_shows_subsequent_loss_of_landlord: The tenant showed that the landlord lost title after the tenant was inducted.

issues.definition: When a returning non-resident owner seeks personal-use eviction and the tenant admitted induction by that owner, the continuing tenant who has not surrendered possession and establishes neither paramount-title attornment nor subsequent loss of the landlord’s title is estopped from denying the landlord’s title, so the ownership-period requirement is met against that tenant.
